## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Vaḍḍhakīsūkarajātaka* (Ja 283) is a story in the Jātaka collection of the Pali Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. According to the traditional opening (*paccuppannavatthu*), the Buddha delivered this teaching while residing at Jetavana with reference to the Elder Dhanuggahatissa (*Dhanuggahatissatthera*) [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. The narrative framework involves Mahākosala, father of King Pasenadi, who granted a village in Kāsi yielding a large revenue as bath-money (*nahānacuṇṇamūla*) to his daughter Kosaladevi upon her marriage to King Bimbisāra; upon Bimbisāra's death at the hands of Ajātasattu, Kosaladevi died of grief, prompting a war over the revenues of that village [Radich 2011; Fausböll 1879]. In the identification of the birth (*samodhāna*), the carpenter's boar (*vaḍḍhakisūkara*) was identified as Dhanuggahatissa, while the Buddha identified himself as the tree devatā (*rukkhadevatā*) [Fausböll 1879].
No cross-language parallels are recorded on SuttaCentral or detected by DharmaNexus. However, DharmaNexus identifies Pali-internal text reuse comprising six matching segments between the verses and the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. Furthermore, modern scholarship notes that the frame narrative concerning the dispute over the bath-money village and the resulting conflict between Ajātasattu and Pasenadi is repeated in the *Tacchasūkara-jātaka* as well as the *Hāritamātā-jātaka* [Radich 2011].
